content.body: # Week 2: Arrays and Strings Overview and Key Concepts for Instructional Delivery ## Lesson Objectives In this lesson, students will explore how data is stored within a computer, specifically focusing on arrays and strings. Key learning outcomes include understanding how a compiler converts source code into machine code, utilizing arrays to store data in back-to-back memory portions, and recognizing that strings are simply arrays of characters. ## Core Concepts: Compiling and Memory Storage Students must recall that a compiler is a specialized program converting source code into machine code. The workflow involves taking source code and processing it through a compiler to generate executable machine code. When discussing memory, emphasize that arrays store values in a sequence, occupying back-to-back portions of memory. For example, an integer array like `int scores[3]` allocates three contiguous memory locations of type `int`. ## Strings as Character Arrays A critical concept is that a `string` is defined as an array of values of type `char`. Instruct students to visualize a string as an array beginning with the first character and ending with a special `NUL character` (represented as `0`). When printing strings, note that ASCII codes are displayed by replacing the `%c` format specifier with `%i`. Students should practice treating strings as arrays by accessing individual characters via indices (e.g., `s[0]`, `s[1]`). It is important to demonstrate that accessing the NUL character at the end of a string is necessary to print all ASCII codes correctly. ## Practical Application: Code Examples Instruct students to write code that declares character variables (`char c1`, `c2`, etc.) and prints them individually versus as a string. Further exercises should involve declaring an array of strings, such as `string words[2]`, to store multiple string literals. Students should modify existing code to iterate through or print specific indices of a string to reinforce the array concept. ## Summary and Next Steps Conclude the session by reviewing the four primary debugging methods and the distinction between command-line arguments and standard input. Ensure students understand that command-line arguments can be passed directly to programs. Prepare for the next lesson by highlighting the topics of string length, exit status, and further command-line argument manipulation.

items.name: Pointers
items.incorrect_belief: A pointer is simply a variable that stores a value, similar to a standard integer or float variable.
items.correction: A pointer is a specific type of variable that stores the memory address of another variable, not the value itself. While a standard variable (like `int n`) holds data (e.g., 50), a pointer (like `int *p`) holds the location in memory where that data resides (e.g., 0x7ffee...). The address-of operator (`&`) retrieves this location, and the dereference operator (`*`) accesses the value at that location.

items.name: Hexadecimal notation
items.incorrect_belief: Hexadecimal numbers used in memory addresses or values are ambiguous and could be mistaken for decimal integers without context.
items.correction: To prevent confusion between hexadecimal values and decimal integers, the C programming convention requires hexadecimal numbers to be prefixed with `0x`. For example, `0x50` explicitly denotes the hexadecimal value 50, whereas `50` is interpreted as the decimal value fifty. This prefix is essential when interpreting memory addresses (which often start with `0x`) and when defining constants in code.

items.name: Dynamic memory allocation
items.incorrect_belief: Memory allocated using `malloc` is automatically freed by the system when the program ends or when the variable goes out of scope, so explicit cleanup is unnecessary.
items.correction: Memory allocated dynamically via `malloc` is not automatically freed. It remains reserved until the programmer explicitly calls `free()` on the pointer. Failure to free this memory results in a memory leak, where resources are consumed but never returned to the system. Tools like Valgrind can detect these leaks and also identify out-of-bounds accesses, such as writing to `x[3]` in an array allocated with size 3.

items.name: Dynamic memory allocation
items.incorrect_belief: Standard C compilers will automatically detect and report memory leaks or out-of-bounds array accesses during normal compilation and execution.
items.correction: Standard C compilers do not automatically detect memory leaks or out-of-bounds errors during normal execution because the C language does not enforce memory safety checks at runtime by default. Developers must use external tools like Valgrind to analyze the program's memory usage. Valgrind can identify issues such as memory leaks (failure to `free` allocated memory) and invalid memory accesses (e.g., accessing `x[3]` when only indices 0, 1, and 2 were allocated).

content.title: Instructor Draft: Week 4 Memory Management & Valgrind Review
content.body: ## Week 4 Overview and Learning Objectives Welcome to Week 4. This lesson covers foundational concepts in memory management, including pixel art, hexadecimal numbering, pointers, strings, pointer arithmetic, string comparison, copying, malloc and Valgrind, garbage values, swapping, overflow, scanf, and file I/O. The primary focus of this session is understanding how pointers provide the ability to access and manipulate data at specific memory locations, and how to use Valgrind to detect memory-related issues in programs utilizing malloc. ### Core Concepts: Pointers and Memory In C, a pointer is a variable that stores the address of something; most succinctly, it is an address in your computer's memory. To visualize this, consider an integer `n` stored in memory. By convention, hexadecimal numbers representing memory locations are prefixed with `0x`. We utilize two powerful operators to interact with memory: the `&` operator, which provides the address of something stored in memory, and the `*` operator, which instructs the compiler to go to a location in memory. For example, `int *p = &n;` creates a pointer `p` that stores the memory address of the integer `n`. Executing code to print this address using `printf` with the `%p` format specifier will return an address beginning with `0x`. ### Memory Allocation and Valgrind When using `malloc` to allocate memory for arrays, it is critical to ensure that the allocated memory is eventually freed. Consider a scenario where an array `x` is allocated with `malloc(3 * sizeof(int))`. This allocates space for indices `0`, `1`, and `2`. If a program attempts to assign a value to `x[3]`, it accesses memory outside the allocated bounds. While the program may not crash immediately, this constitutes a memory error. Additionally, if the program terminates without calling `free` on the allocated pointer, memory is lost. Valgrind is a tool designed to check for such memory-related issues. By running `valgrind ./program_name`, instructors can generate a report identifying where memory has been lost, including out-of-bounds writes and unfreed allocations. For instance, Valgrind can reveal attempts to assign values at indices beyond the allocated size and confirm that the allocated memory was never released. ### Summary In this lesson, we delved into the mechanics of pointers, hexadecimal representation of memory, and the use of Valgrind to ensure robust memory management. Understanding these concepts is essential for preventing garbage values, overflow errors, and memory leaks in C programs.

content.title: Project: Basic Circuit Analysis via KVL and KCL
content.body: Students will analyze a provided lumped circuit diagram to determine all branch voltages and currents. The project requires students to first select a reference node (ground) and label the remaining node voltages as primary unknowns. Next, students must write Kirchhoff's Current Law (KCL) equations for all non-ground nodes, substituting device laws (Ohm's Law for resistors, constraints for sources) and Kirchhoff's Voltage Law (KVL) where necessary. Finally, students must solve the resulting system of linear equations to find the node voltages and back-solve for the branch currents. Students must strictly adhere to the 'associated variables' discipline, ensuring current is defined as positive entering the positive voltage terminal to correctly calculate power consumption. The project may also involve simplifying sub-circuits using series/parallel combination rules for resistors and sources before applying the full KVL/KCL method if the circuit topology permits.

content.title: Instructor Draft: Fundamentals of Circuit Analysis Methods
content.body: This lecture introduces the foundational techniques for analyzing linear circuits, focusing on the relationship between Kirchhoff's laws and element characteristics. The primary objective of circuit analysis is to determine all element voltages and currents. This is achieved by establishing a system of equations based on three core steps: writing element voltage-current (v-i) relationships derived from the lumped circuit abstraction, applying Kirchhoff's Current Law (KCL) to all nodes, and applying Kirchhoff's Voltage Law (KVL) to all loops. While this method generates a large number of unknowns and equations, it provides a systematic approach to solving complex networks. A specific application of this general method is Node Analysis, which involves selecting a reference node (ground), labeling the voltages of remaining nodes with respect to ground as primary unknowns, and writing KCL equations for all non-ground nodes. Once node voltages are solved, branch voltages and currents can be back-calculated. Alternatively, circuits can be analyzed by applying element combination rules, such as combining resistors in series or parallel, or using current and voltage source transformations. Throughout these analyses, it is critical to maintain the discipline of associated variables, where current is defined as positive entering the positive voltage terminal of an element to correctly calculate power consumption.

content.title: Course FAQs: Basic Circuit Analysis Methods
content.body: What are the primary methods for circuit analysis covered in this course? The course introduces three main methods: Method 1 is the basic KVL and KCL method; Method 2 involves applying element combination rules; and Method 3 is node analysis, which is a particular application of the KVL and KCL method. What is the goal of the basic KVL and KCL method? The goal is to find all element voltages (v's) and currents (i's) by writing element v-i relationships, writing KCL for all nodes, writing KVL for all loops, and then solving the resulting system of equations. What are the specific steps for the basic KVL and KCL method? The steps are: 1) Select a reference node (ground) from which voltages are measured. 2) Label the voltages of the remaining nodes with respect to ground; these are the primary unknowns. 3) Write KCL for all but the ground node, substituting device laws and KVL. 4) Solve for node voltages. 5) Back solve for branch voltages and currents, which are the secondary unknowns. What are the element relationships for resistors, voltage sources, and current sources? For a resistor, the relationship is v = iR. For a voltage source, the voltage is constant (v = V). For a current source, the current is constant (i = I). What is the 'associated variables discipline' for calculating power? Power consumed by an element is positive when the current is taken to be positive going into the positive voltage terminal. Under this convention, power consumed is calculated as p = vi. How do Maxwell's equations relate to KVL and KCL? Maxwell's equations simplify to algebraic KVL and KCL under the Lumped Matter Discipline (LMD).

content.title: Course FAQs: Introduction to Pharmacology
content.body: What are the core definitions of agonist and antagonist? An agonist is a drug that binds to a receptor and produces a characteristic effect, which can be a full or partial effect depending on the maximal response. An antagonist binds to the receptor without causing an effect, thereby preventing an active substance from gaining access. Antagonists may be competitive, non-competitive, or irreversible. What is the relationship between dose and response? The dose-response relationship is fundamental to drug effect; generally, as the dose of a drug increases, the response should increase. When effect is plotted against the log dose, the curve is usually sigmoidal. How do we distinguish between potency and efficacy? Potency refers to the dose (or molar concentration) required to produce a specific intensity of effect, often specified by the ED50 (median effective dose). Efficacy, also called maximal efficacy or intrinsic activity, is the maximum effect a drug is capable of producing. A potent drug may have low efficacy, and a highly efficacious drug may have low potency. For clinicians, efficacy is often more important than potency. What is the difference between affinity and selectivity? Affinity refers to the strength of binding between a drug and its receptor, quantified by the dissociation constant kD. Selectivity refers to the separation between desired and undesired effects of a drug. Ideally, a drug is completely specific, but many therapeutic agents produce dose-related side effects near their therapeutic range. What is the role of the unbound drug in distribution? After administration, the unbound drug follows its concentration gradient to distribute into peripheral tissues. Some tissues contain the target site, while others act as non-specific binding reservoirs. The total volume of distribution determines the equilibrium concentration of the drug after a specified dose. What are the key pharmacokinetic processes involved? content.title: Pharmacokinetics I & II: Project Directions and Learning Outcomes
content.body: This project requires students to analyze the relationship between pharmacokinetic parameters and plasma drug concentrations. Students must explain how dose, bioavailability, rate of absorption, apparent volume of distribution, total clearance, and elimination half-life affect plasma concentrations following a single dose. The project involves calculating the apparent volume of distribution by extrapolating plasma concentration data to time zero and determining total clearance based on the mass of drug eliminated per unit time. Additionally, students will investigate the effect of infusions or multiple dosing on the time-course of plasma concentrations, specifically focusing on steady-state conditions where the plasma concentration is directly proportional to the input rate and inversely proportional to total plasma clearance. Students must also determine renal clearance by measuring the amount of drug excreted in urine over a specific time interval and interpolating plasma concentration at the midpoint of that interval.

content.title: Instructor Draft: Pharmacokinetic Principles and Calculations
content.body: This module covers the fundamental parameters of pharmacokinetics, focusing on how drug dose, bioavailability, and elimination kinetics influence plasma concentrations. Students will learn to calculate the apparent volume of distribution (Vd) by extrapolating plasma concentration data to time zero, where Vd equals the total dose divided by the initial concentration (C0). The concept of total clearance (ClT) is defined as the volume of plasma completely cleared of drug per unit time, which can be determined by dividing the mass of drug eliminated per unit time by the plasma concentration. The relationship between these parameters is critical for understanding steady-state conditions; specifically, the plasma concentration at steady-state (Css) is directly proportional to the input rate of the drug and inversely proportional to its total plasma clearance. Furthermore, the elimination half-life is directly proportional to Vd and inversely proportional to total clearance, meaning that for a given clearance, a higher volume of distribution results in a longer half-life. Students must also be able to explain how the area under the plasma concentration vs. time curve (AUC) depends on the dose, the fraction of dose absorbed (bioavailability), and total clearance, noting that bioavailability is experimentally determined by comparing the AUC of a specific dosage form to that of an intravenous dose under conditions of complete absorption.
